A brand archetype report & differentiation strategy for Kurtis Coaching & Consulting · Kurt Rudsinski
Brand Archetype Report Identity · Voice · Landscape · Differentiation · Visual Direction · November 2026
What this report is: the result of Kurt Rudsinski’s brand archetype assessment for Kurtis Coaching & Consulting, scored with Skyway’s weighted 37-point engine across all twelve archetypes, then translated into an identity, a voice, a read of the national coaching market, five ways to pull away from it, and three directions for how the brand should look. Twelve scored answers sit behind it, every one of them printed verbatim under “Their answers.”
01 · Brand Identity

The coach who asks what the growth is for

Your discovery returned two archetypes a single point apart, and the engine is right to name both. You understand businesses, and you want the people inside them to get somewhere. Sage and Explorer are the identity together. Caregiver, one point further back, is the manner: you come alongside. The combination is a coach who can install structure and still ask the question structure never asks: what is all of this for?

Sage · The What
Clarity is the product

An operating system that “simplifies and prioritizes” so a leadership team makes better decisions faster. That is a Sage’s deliverable: understanding, made usable.

  • You chose “wise and knowledgeable” as the brand’s character, the Sage’s own words.
  • You reward people who “bring deep insight and thoughtful, informed perspectives.”
  • “Insightful” and “simple” are two of your three strengths, and doubt is the first fear you named.
Explorer · The Why
One life. Make it count.

Your motto is the Explorer’s, verbatim. Your setting is rugged mountains. You face problems “with adventurous curiosity.” The destination is a life the owner actually gets to live.

  • “You only get one life, make it count” is the Explorer’s own motto in the quiz, and you chose it over eleven others.
  • Curiosity, not conquest, is your problem-solving posture. Hero scored zero.
  • Work/life balance, time with family and friends, the “More”: freedom is the promised outcome.
Caregiver · The How
Alongside, not above

“I come alongside CEOs.” “Take care of the people.” “Fill capacity gaps.” You described a Caregiver’s delivery three times without using the word.

  • Your symbol is touching hands. Among your fears is ingratitude, the Caregiver’s own, beside loneliness.
  • “Approachable” leads your list of strengths.
  • The fractional-executive offer is the Caregiver taken to its limit: you will sit in the empty chair.

At the core, you’re a Sage and an Explorer.

The Sage’s drive is understanding; the Explorer’s is freedom. Most brands carry one and borrow the other. You carry both at full weight, Sage 7 and Explorer 6, and the pairing is the identity rather than a primary with a flavour. It shows up in the business exactly as you described it: a leadership team gets an operating system that makes the next decision obvious (Sage), and the owner gets back the evenings, the weekends and the marriage the business was eating (Explorer). Lean into: plain explanations over frameworks, the forward question (“then what?”) in every conversation, and freedom, not growth, as the thing you promise.

Caregiver is how it is delivered.

Caregiver 5 is close enough to shape every interaction and far enough back that it should never be the headline. The category already leads with care; every peer group sells a safe room. Yours lives in the verbs. You come alongside. You take care of the people and let the income statement take care of itself. You will, if the seat is empty, sit in it as a fractional executive. Lean into: presence in the Monday meeting, patience with the team that is not ready yet, and the fractional seat as proof that “alongside” is not a figure of speech.

Why the combination is one-of-a-kind.

The twelve archetypes group into four families by core human drive, and 15 of your 37 points land in the Spiritual family (Sage 7, Explorer 6, Innocent 2): meaning, understanding and freedom. Yet your stated purpose is “to provide structure for others,” a Structural answer, and your gradient, strengths and animal all landed outside the Spiritual family too, which is why the engine flagged the family check at 0 of 3. That is not a contradiction. It is the whole brand: a Spiritual head on Structural hands. The soul of the thing is why; the product is how. Implementers sell the how and go quiet on the why. Faith-driven peer groups sell the why and cannot install the how. You are the bridge, and the family check is the evidence.

The one thing to make unmistakable
Every operating system promises clarity, accountability and alignment, in the same words, to the same owner. Yours is the only one that asks what the abundance is for, and then helps the family get it too.
“Clear-eyed about the business. Convicted about what it’s for.”
The identity in one line: you understand how a company runs, you want its owner free, and you stay in the room until both are true
One role sits underneath: Magician. “Business Coach” is the character you chose, and in the engine it is the Magician’s role: the person through whom a company becomes a different company. Magician 4 is real, but it is the job title, not the voice. Transformation is what happens to the client; it is never how you talk.

The guardrail: Sage and Explorer lead together; Caregiver carries them. Teach before you preach, ask before you prescribe, and never hustle. If a line sounds like a seminar, a sermon or a pep rally, it’s the wrong line. You’re the one person who is none of the three.

Sage and Explorer at the heart. Care in the delivery.

A brand is strongest when it knows exactly what leads. Yours leads with two, and the numbers say so plainly: Sage 7 and Explorer 6, one point apart, which the engine calls “present both.” Caregiver sits at 5, one more point back. Below that the field drops away, and two archetypes a coach is usually assumed to carry, Hero and Outlaw, scored nothing at all.

The family check fired at 0 of 3, meaning your gradient, strengths and animal all landed outside the Spiritual family that won (Structural, Structural, Connector). Scored with Skyway’s 37-point engine (v2.0), the same weighted read used on every archetype report we ship. Every complete response totals exactly 37, and yours did. Figures are points of 37, not percentages, so they compare directly across reports.
Sage · in your words

Your brand’s character is “wise and knowledgeable.” You reward “deep insight and thoughtful, informed perspectives.” You help teams “make better decisions more efficiently.” Understanding, made simple, is the product.

Explorer · your why

Your motto, “you only get one life, make it count,” is the Explorer’s. Your setting is rugged mountains, and you face problems “with adventurous curiosity.” The outcome you keep describing is an owner who gets a life back.

Caregiver · how you deliver

“I come alongside CEOs.” Your symbol is touching hands, your first strength is “approachable,” and your fears include ingratitude and loneliness. You take care of the people, including when that means filling the seat yourself.

The whole brand, in one line

Your tagline: “It’s More than the Bottom Line.” The Sage’s clarity about what the numbers are, the Explorer’s insistence on what they are for, and the Caregiver’s instruction to take care of the people first.

Sage · 7UnderstandingCo-lead. “Wise and knowledgeable,” “insightful,” “simple,” and a fear of doubt. The operating system is understanding you can run a Monday meeting on. → Clear, considered, plain-spoken.
Explorer · 6FreedomCo-lead. The motto, the mountains, “adventurous curiosity.” Freedom from being the bottleneck, freedom to be home. → Curious, forward, unhurried.
Caregiver · 5ServiceThe How. “Come alongside,” touching hands, “take care of the people.” Lives in the verbs and the fractional seat, stays out of the tagline. → Present, patient, alongside.
Magician · 4PowerThe role, not the voice. “Business Coach” is the Magician’s character in the engine: the person through whom a company becomes a different company.
Lover · 4IntimacyReal and quiet. Marriages, friendships, the “personal and professional relationships” you named as an outcome. In the stories, never the pitch.
Everyman · 3BelongingThe Dolphin and “approachable.” You meet owners where they are, but you’re the one who has run the P&L, and the brand shouldn’t pretend otherwise.
Creator · 3InnovationPresent only as craft: the system, the templates, the quarterly rhythm. Not an identity driver.
Ruler · 2Control“To provide structure for others.” Structure is what you hand over, not how you hold the room. Keep it low; the implementer camp lives here.
Innocent · 2SafetyThe quiet faith note and the simple life on the other side of the work. A destination, not a driver.
Jester · 1EnjoymentFaint. A warm, dry touch that keeps a hard quarterly from feeling like a tribunal. Never the lead.
Outlaw · 0LiberationNot you. You don’t burn systems down; you install better ones. Clarifying.
Hero · 0MasteryNot you, and the most useful zero on the chart. No grind, no 10x, no war room. The hustle coach is the one voice in the category you never borrow.

Where the weight sits: Spiritual 15 · Structural 10 · Connector 8 · Legacy 4. Spiritual carries 15 of 37, and that is the truest sentence in this section: the brand is about meaning first, mechanics second, and it delivers the meaning through the mechanics.

03 · Core Purpose

So the business serves the life it was built for

Kurtis Coaching & Consulting exists for the owner of a five-to-ten-million-dollar company who is working too much, is absent from the people he loves, and has a leadership team that talks past itself. You give that team an operating system that simplifies and prioritizes, so decisions get made and the owner stops being the bottleneck. Then you ask the question the growth was always for: when the business has abundance, what are you going to do with it? Faith, family, business, in that order. Take care of the people, and the income statement usually takes care of itself.

It’s the Sage’s purpose, understanding sets you free, and the Explorer’s, one life, make it count, delivered the Caregiver’s way: alongside, and with the people first.

Alternates to react to

Take care of the people. The numbers tend to follow.

Growth you never have to apologize to your family for.

Structure for the business. Priorities for the life. A reason for both.

04 · Voice & Personality

Say the simple true thing. Then stay in the room.

If the brand were a person: a former executive who has carried a P&L and the Sunday-night dread that comes with it, now sitting across a diner table from a founder. He asks about your daughter’s season before your third quarter, draws the next ninety days in four boxes on the back of the placemat, and says grace before the eggs without expecting anyone else to bow their head. He has read the business books. He quotes none of them.

Clear

We are plain-spoken, structured, simple  ·  not academic, acronym-heavy, or drunk on our own framework.
“Three priorities this quarter. Not seven. Three.”

Curious

We are forward-looking, question-first, unafraid of the awkward one  ·  not restless, novelty-chasing, or vague about the next step.
“Say the business doubles. Then what? Who gets that time?”

Alongside

We are present, patient, in the Monday meeting  ·  not pitying, soft on accountability, or building a client who needs us forever.
“I’ll sit in the leadership meeting until it runs without me. That’s the goal.”

Convicted

We are open about faith, unhurried, unembarrassed  ·  not preachy, exclusionary, or performing it for the camera.
“If my faith is a dealbreaker, that’s okay. Better we both know on the first call.”

On the dials: simple over clever · alongside over above · asking over telling · people over numbers, never instead of them · convicted over loud · calm over hype · the owner’s language over the framework’s.

Website hero line

“Predictable growth for the business. Priorities for the life. An operating system for both, and a coach who stays in the room until it runs without him.”

LinkedIn post

“Your leadership team doesn’t need more meetings. It needs one that works. Here’s the ninety-minute version, and why the first thing we cut is the agenda.”

Discovery call opener

“Before the numbers: what does a good Saturday look like right now, and how many of them did you get last quarter?”

The guardrail: the authority comes from having run a business and from the simplicity of the advice, never from the certification or the volume. If a line needs a trademark symbol or an exclamation point to land, it isn’t the right line.
Part II · The Strategy

Now that we know who you are, here’s how you win.

The identity only matters if it opens a lane the market can’t follow you into. So we mapped the national market for business coaching around the owner you described, the five-to-ten-million-dollar company with twenty people and a founder who is never home, and sorted it into the three camps that owner actually shortlists.

05 · Competitive Landscape

Three camps. None of them own your lane.

The market sorts into the operating-system implementers, the faith-driven peer groups, and the executive coaches and fractional firms. Each owns a piece of what you do. None of them owns the whole of it, and none of them says what you say in the first sentence. (Read from each brand’s public positioning on 2 November 2026, scoped to national reach, and to be validated with you on review. You named EOS implementers, proprietary business coaches, C12 and Acumen; we added the adjacent names your ideal owner would also be comparing.)

Camp One
The operating-system implementers
WhoCertified EOS Implementers® (EOS Worldwide), Scaling Up coaches, Pinnacle guides, Bloom Growth coaches. Your own licensed system sits in this camp, which is exactly why you can’t sound like it. Our readRuler + Sage. A proprietary framework, a certification, a quarterly cadence, and a trademark on every noun. VoiceSystematic and promissory: “Vision, Traction, Healthy,” “get a grip on your business,” “unlock the full potential,” “transform grind into growth.” You winThey install the system and leave the life alone. You install it in the business and in the household, and you ask what the Traction is for.
Camp Two
The faith-driven peer groups
WhoC12 Business Forums, Convene, Truth At Work, Acumen, and the chapter-based forums for Christian owners Our readEveryman + Caregiver. A confidential room, a chair, a curriculum, one day a month with non-competing peers. VoiceWarm and communal: “close the gap between your faith and your business,” “lead whole,” “the power of the room.” You winThey give the owner a room once a month. You’re in the business the other twenty-nine days, with the whole leadership team, and when the seat is empty, in the seat. Not a rival so much as a referral partner: the forum is where the owner goes to think; you’re where the thinking gets implemented.
Camp Three
The executive coaches and fractional firms
WhoVistage and its Chairs, the sea of solo executive coaches, and the fractional COO and CFO shops Our readRuler + Hero. Scale, credentials and performance language; the 1:1 is a feature of the membership, not the product. VoiceAssured and statistical: “the world’s largest,” “member companies last 4x longer,” “work on the business, not in it.” You winThey sell the network and the numbers. You sell one person who will say the quiet part out loud: the business is supposed to serve the family, not the other way round.
The open lane
One coach who is all three at once: implementation-grade, faith-explicit, and in the room.

The implementers can’t speak to the life, the peer groups can’t install the system, and the executive coaches won’t say what the money is for. Every one of them claims clarity, accountability and alignment, in the same words, and the owner has no way to referee the frameworks from the outside. He can referee this: who asked about his Saturdays, who was in the Monday meeting, and who said “faith” before he had to.

06 · Differentiation Strategy

Five ways to pull away

Each pillar targets the open lane, and each is something the brand should actively say, not just imply.

Lead with the question nobody else asks.

The implementers promise traction. The peer groups promise a room. The executive coaches promise results. Not one of them opens with what the growth is for. You already have the line, “It’s More than the Bottom Line,” and the sentence behind it: when the business has abundance, how will you use it for a greater good? Make that the first thing a prospect reads, not the last thing you mention.

In the brandThe tagline sits under the wordmark on every surface. The website opens with the question, not the credentials. Every case story ends with what the owner did with the time and the money, never with the revenue number alone.

Run one operating system for the business and the life.

Your own description draws the lane: the leadership team gets structure that simplifies and prioritizes, and then the CEO gets the same thing for his personal life. No implementer offers the second half. No peer group can deliver the first. Name it as one system with two sides, with faith, family and business as the three rocks it is built to protect, in that order.

In the brandCall the personal side something, and put it on the services page beside the business side with equal weight. Use the same vocabulary for both: priorities, rhythm, accountability, next ninety days.

Be in the room, and when needed, in the seat.

“Alongside” is your verb, and the fractional-executive offer is what makes it more than a sentiment. A C12 chair sees the owner one day a month. A Vistage group meets monthly. You sit in the leadership meeting, run the quarterly, and, if the company has a capacity gap, fill the chair until it doesn’t. That is a category of its own, and the brand should stop apologizing for the fractional work as a “lastly.”

In the brandPromote the fractional seat from the footnote to the proof. “Coach, implementer, and when you need it, the executive in the seat.” Show the Monday meeting in the imagery, not the keynote stage.

Make faith the first filter, not the fine print.

You said it yourself: if faith turns a prospect away, that is a good first filter. The peer groups put faith in the name and then speak in corporate wellness language. The implementers avoid it entirely. You can be the one coach who says it plainly on the first page, in the manner you described, subtle evidence without being in anyone’s face, and lets the right owner self-select.

In the brandA single, unhurried sentence about faith in the hero section and the bio, in your voice, never a verse in the header. Keep the KCC mark’s quiet nod to it. No fish, no crosses, no stock church imagery.

Keep it simple, and let the income statement take care of itself.

Hero scored zero, and that is the most useful number on your chart. The coaching category runs on intensity: 10x, grind, war rooms, extreme ownership. You chose “simple” as a strength and “approachable” as the first one. Your promise is fewer priorities, calmer meetings, and a leadership team that stops needing you. Say less than the competition, and say it more plainly, and the contrast does the selling.

In the brandThree-item lists, never seven. One sentence per outcome. No countdown timers, no “crush,” no exclamation points. If a competitor would print it in bold red, you print it in plain blue.

Your strategic sweet spot
The coach who comes alongside.

A Sage’s clarity, an Explorer’s compass, and a Caregiver’s patience: structure for the business, priorities for the life, and a bigger reason for both.

07 · Visual Identity · Concept Strategies

Three ways to look the part

Direction, not decoration: three strategic concepts for the brand’s visual identity, each true to Sage × Explorer with Caregiver in the delivery, and each built from the colours and the style you actually chose. We’ll design the boards once a direction is picked.

Concept A
Quiet authority

The clearest voice in the room, stated with restraint.

A minimal, editorial system: cobalt on white, generous space, a warm humanist sans for the work and a serif reserved for the lines that carry conviction. The look of advice you can trust because it isn’t shouting.

Pros
  • Matches your “modern, clean, minimalist” brief exactly
  • Sage-first; reads credible to a CFO and a pastor alike
  • A clean foil to the trademark-heavy implementer look and the hustle look
Tradeoffs
  • Needs warmth from photography and voice or it drifts corporate
  • Underplays the Explorer; the compass has to come from the words
Concept B
Open water

The horizon is the promise.

Explorer-led: the blue-into-cyan gradient you chose becomes a horizon line that runs through everything, with wide landscape photography (your rugged mountains, open water, early light) and violet reserved for depth and dusk. Movement without hype.

Pros
  • Tells the freedom story on sight; owns “one life, make it count”
  • Ownable, because nobody in any camp looks like this
  • The Dolphin and the mountains, your own picks, become the image library
Tradeoffs
  • Gradients have to be handled carefully or the brand reads as software
  • Landscape imagery can feel like a retreat centre; needs people in it
Concept C
At the table

Alongside, made visible.

Caregiver-led: warm humanist type, rounded forms, and photography of real leadership teams mid-meeting, with you in the frame but never at the head of the table. The brand as the person who showed up.

Pros
  • Lowest barrier for an owner who flinches at anything that smells like a seminar
  • Makes “in the room” and the fractional seat literal
  • Extends naturally to the personal-side offer
Tradeoffs
  • Drifts straight into the peer-group look: every forum uses people around a table
  • Underplays the Sage and the Explorer, your two co-leads
  • Depends on a real photo library, not stock

The color thinking

You chose violet, cobalt and white, and the pairing is better than it first looks. Cobalt is the Sage’s natural ground: calm, considered, trustworthy. It is also the category’s default; nearly every advisory and peer-group brand lives in some blue, so cobalt alone disappears. Violet is what makes the pair ownable, and in a faith-explicit brand it carries a quiet second meaning: it is the liturgical colour of Advent and Lent, royalty and reflection. That is the kind of subtle evidence you said you wanted, in the colour rather than in the consumer’s face. Keep it as depth, never as the lead.

Two collisions to manage. First, run cobalt and violet as flat fields, not as a gradient: blue-to-violet is the stock gradient of software and app branding, and you already resell a software platform, so the pair as a gradient reads as a Bloom Growth sub-brand rather than as you. Your own gradient pick was blue into cyan, and that is the right one: cyan for the light and the horizon, violet for the shadow. Second, let white do most of the work. The minimalist brief and the Caregiver both want air; aim for white carrying the majority of every surface, cobalt for structure, violet for emphasis.

Your avoid list is the right one and worth saying out loud. Gold is the one colour a faith-driven brand that insists it is not about the money must never touch; rust and moss are the earthy palette the peer-group camp leans on. All three stay out. When the Bloom Growth brand guide arrives, the test is simple: the KCC palette has to sit beside it on the same page without looking like it reports to it.

The type thinking

You asked for “warm and humanist” in a modern, clean system, and that is the right ask for Sage × Explorer delivered by a Caregiver. The workhorse should be a humanist sans with real warmth, Mulish or Nunito Sans, set with generous leading and never in all caps for anything longer than a label. Beside it, one serif with character, Fraunces or Lora, reserved for the sentences that carry conviction: the tagline, the pullquotes, the one line about faith. “It’s More than the Bottom Line” is a serif sentence.

Two faces to avoid. Geometric sans (Poppins, Montserrat) push the brand toward the software camp, which the colour section just worked to escape. Heavy condensed and slab faces are the hustle coach’s wardrobe, and Hero scored zero. The KCC monogram you like should be re-drawn in the chosen sans so the quiet faith reference in the mark survives the move.

Our lean: Concept A, carrying Concept B’s horizon. A quiet, editorial, cobalt-and-white system that keeps the Sage’s credibility, with the blue-into-cyan horizon line and wide-open imagery giving the Explorer a visible promise, and real photography of leadership teams, not stock, supplying the warmth Concept C would otherwise bring.
08 · Summary

A Sage and an Explorer, walking alongside.

Clear about how a business runs, convicted about what it’s for, and patient enough to stay in the room until the owner gets his life back. In a market split between frameworks that stop at the office door, forums that meet once a month, and coaches who never say what the money is for, you are the one who installs the structure, asks the bigger question, and takes care of the people first. It’s more than the bottom line.

The business
Describe what you do
I am a coach. I help businesses and their leaders achieve predictable and sustainable growth, improve their work / life balance and improve their personal and professional relationships. I do this by helping leadership teams implement an operating system that simplifies and prioritizes better then left by themselves so they make better decisions more efficiently.
